title: CompTIA A+ vs Network+ vs Security+: Which First?
subtitle: The CompTIA trio: where to start and in what order in 2026

pros: The ultimate entry point into IT: no prerequisites, designed for true beginners.
Covers the practical side of support — hardware, OS, mobile, troubleshooting — useful from your first helpdesk job.
Recruiters recognize it as proof that you can fix and configure a machine.
An essential foundation before Network+ if you've never opened a PC or managed a workstation.
cons: Two exams to pass (Core 1 + Core 2) — the total cost climbs fast (~$500).
Very broad but shallow: it skims many topics without mastering any.
Tier-1 support salaries plateau quickly — it's a springboard, not a destination.
Valued less in Europe than in the US, where helpdesk is a huge market.
certs.bestFor: You're starting IT from zero and targeting a first support / helpdesk job.

pros: The vendor-neutral networking foundation: TCP/IP, the OSI model, subnetting, VLANs, routing — the base for everything else.
The perfect bridge before the CCNA if you want to specialize in Cisco networking.
Deeper than A+ while staying approachable — a good effort-to-recognition ratio.
An implicit prerequisite for security: you can't secure a network you don't understand.
cons: A single but dense exam — subnetting trips up many candidates.
Vendor-neutral = general; an all-Cisco employer will often prefer the CCNA directly.
Less 'sellable' on its own on a résumé than Security+, which is in very high demand today.
Little graded hands-on practice — it's multiple choice, not live configuration.
certs.bestFor: You want to understand networking in depth before targeting the CCNA or security.

pros: The most in-demand entry-level cybersecurity cert — it appears in most junior SOC job postings.
DoD 8570/8140 approved: a must for US defense / contractor roles.
The best starting salary of the trio — security pays better than support or pure networking.
A direct springboard to CySA+, PenTest+ or cloud security certs (SC-200, AWS Security).
cons: Assumes solid networking basics — taking it without Network+ (or equivalent) hurts.
Broad and conceptual: lots of vocabulary, little graded hands-on work.
The junior cyber market is saturated with certified candidates who lack experience.
Renewal every 3 years (CEUs or retake) — ongoing upkeep required.
certs.bestFor: You're targeting cybersecurity (SOC, analyst, compliance) and already have networking basics.

verdicts.profile: You're starting from zero, with no IT experience at all.
verdicts.why: A+ is the only one of the three designed for true beginners; it makes you employable in helpdesk and lays the hardware / OS foundations.

verdicts.profile: You're already comfortable using a PC and want to understand how machines communicate.
verdicts.why: You can skip A+: Network+ lays the TCP/IP / OSI / routing foundation you need before any networking or security specialization.

verdicts.profile: Your clear goal is cybersecurity (SOC, analyst, compliance).
verdicts.why: It's the entry-level cyber cert most cited in job postings; go straight for it if your networking basics are already solid.

verdicts.profile: You want the best starting salary for the fewest exams.
verdicts.why: Security pays better than support or pure networking, and Security+ is a single exam versus A+'s two.

verdicts.profile: You're targeting a defense or contractor (DoD) role.
verdicts.why: Security+ is DoD 8570/8140 approved — often a contractual prerequisite that neither A+ nor Network+ covers.

verdicts.profile: You plan to move on to the Cisco CCNA next.
verdicts.why: Network+ is the ideal vendor-neutral springboard before the CCNA: you arrive at Cisco with OSI, subnetting and VLANs already mastered.

verdicts.profile: You're undecided and want the safest order to do all three.
verdicts.why: The canonical sequence remains A+ → Network+ → Security+: each prepares the next, and it's the path recruiters recognize.

tldr: A+ if you're starting from zero, Network+ for the networking foundation, Security+ if you're targeting cyber — and in that order if you do all three.
